name: Weighing the Scientific Consensus
title: Weighing the Scientific Consensus
answer: Weighing the scientific consensus means judging how much agreement exists across a body of research on a defined question, rather than treating any single paper as decisive. The site's library of 135 research papers and 11,075 extracted claims provides a structured base for this assessment. The focus is on the direction and strength of evidence, not on popularity or citation counts. This work sits within literature review and evidence synthesis, where the goal is a defensible summary of what the research as a whole supports.

sections.body: Weighing the scientific consensus means judging how much agreement exists across a body of research on a defined question, rather than treating any single paper as decisive. The site's library of 135 research papers and 11,075 extracted claims provides a structured base for this assessment. The focus is on the direction and strength of evidence, not on popularity or citation counts. This work sits within literature review and evidence synthesis, where the goal is a defensible summary of what the research as a whole supports.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a curated, static evidence base rather than a live search engine. The site's catalogue of 805 scientific models and 732 AI tools supports comparison of methods, but consensus weighing itself depends on the extracted claims and the original papers they come from. No external consensus search tool is used; the infrastructure is the library and its claim index. This keeps the process reproducible and tied to source documents.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Researchers extract claims from papers, then compare those claims across studies for agreement, contradiction, and replication. Each claim is checked against the original paper, and the site links to that paper rather than to any third party search tool. Weight is given to study design, sample size, and independence of evidence, not to the number of papers alone. The result is a structured view of where the field converges and where it remains divided.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance is central because every claim must be traceable to its source paper, and the site never links to the Consensus search tool. Risks include citation bias, selective reporting, and the appearance of consensus where only a few studies exist. Rights and reuse depend on the original papers' terms, so the site treats its library as a reference collection, not a republished corpus. Reviewers are expected to flag conflicts of interest and unpublished or retracted work.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more structured claim databases that can be updated as new papers are added to the library. Automated extraction and comparison may speed up the work, but human judgment will still be needed to weigh study quality and context. Over time, the site's 11,075 extracted claims could grow into a living map of agreement and disagreement across AI research. The goal is a clearer, more honest picture of what the scientific community actually supports.
